## A reader's question

After [Nothing From Outside, Everything From Inside](../2026-10-23-nothing-from-outside/index.qmd), a reader sent me a question I could not stop thinking about:

> If two observers inside the same closed universe each keep their own records, do they always end up agreeing on one world?

My first answer was one word: no. That was true, but it was too short. "No" sounds like the two observers live in different worlds and that is the end of it. What I actually believe is more interesting, and this essay is the longer answer.

In the last essay the observer came in to rescue the universe from having only one state. But I only ever put one observer in. The question is what happens with two.

I am still not a physicist. This is still curiosity.

## Nobody holds the master copy

The ordinary picture goes like this. There is one world, out there. Each observer takes notes on it. If two observers disagree, at least one of them made a mistake, and you can find out who by checking against the world.

In a closed universe that last step has nowhere to happen. There is no outside, so there is no referee standing there with the master copy. The previous essay said that the view from nowhere returns one state, which is to say nothing. So the world cannot be the thing that guarantees agreement. Any agreement has to be produced from inside, by the observers themselves.

That is the real reason for my "no". Not that observers must disagree, but that nothing is there to *make* them agree in advance.

## Two observers, two pictures

The first way two records can differ is the simplest one, and it came from the last essay. A bigger observer, one that can hold more, sees a richer universe. A smaller one sees a blurrier one.

So their records are not the same. If you lay one over the other, pixel by pixel, they disagree almost everywhere. But that is the wrong comparison. The small observer simply did not record the fine detail. On the detail it did record, the large-scale shapes, the two agree.

![**Figure 1.** Two observers, two pictures. The same toy universe as in the previous essay, recorded by a small observer and a large one. Laid over each other, the records differ almost everywhere (right). Read the large record at the small one's scale and it matches the small record exactly. Below: disagreement against the size of the smaller observer, compared naively (red) and at the coarser scale (blue). In this toy the blue line is zero by construction; the point is what "agree" has to mean. The code is in [figs.py](figs.py).](figures/fig01.png){fig-alt="Four square images of a glowing web. The first is blurry; the second is sharp with thin filaments; the third, the sharp one blurred, looks identical to the first; the fourth, in grey, shows where the first two differ, mostly along the filaments. Below, a red curve of disagreement falls from about 1 to 0 as the smaller observer grows, while a blue line stays at zero."}

This is a small point but it matters for the rest. "Do they agree?" only has a meaning on the questions both of them can ask. A blurry record and a sharp record do not contradict each other. One of them is just shorter.

## When records meet

The second way is deeper, and it is where quantum mechanics comes in.

The physicist Eugene Wigner imagined it in 1961. A friend sits in a closed laboratory and measures an electron: up or down. She writes down the result. Wigner stands outside the sealed lab. As long as nothing leaks out, quantum mechanics tells Wigner to describe the whole lab, friend and notebook included, as still in a superposition of "saw up" and "saw down." The friend has one result. Wigner has a description with both. Two observers, two different accounts, and for now neither is wrong.

For decades this was a thought experiment for seminars. Then it got sharper. In 2018 Frauchiger and Renner built an extended version with two friends and two Wigners, and showed that if every observer reasons with quantum mechanics and treats the others' conclusions as facts, they reach a contradiction. In 2020 a team led by Kok-Wei Bong turned a related version into a real experiment with photons standing in for the friends. Its conclusion is careful but strong: you cannot keep all of these at once, that observed events are absolute facts for everyone, that no influence travels faster than light, and that experimenters choose their settings freely. Something on that list has to go.

So quantum mechanics does not promise that every observer's record is a fact for every other observer. That is the "no" again, now with experiments behind it.

But look at what happens when Wigner opens the door and asks his friend what she saw. Everything changes. Now there is an interaction between them, and quantum mechanics is very firm about interactions: if two records are about the same thing and they are brought together, they are correlated. Measure an electron, and measure it again right away: you get the same answer. Ask the friend, and her answer matches her notebook. The paradoxes all live in the stretch of time *before* the comparison, when the descriptions are kept apart.

Carlo Rovelli's relational quantum mechanics, which I mentioned last time, says properties exist only relative to other systems. Critics asked: then how do two observers ever share anything? In 2022 Emily Adlam and Rovelli answered by adding one rule, which they call cross-perspective links. Roughly: when one observer checks another observer's record of something, what they find matches what the other recorded. In other words, consistency is not a property of the world seen from above. It is a rule about meetings.

That is what I meant in my reply. Two observers can tell different stories while they are apart. When they meet and compare, quantum mechanics makes the stories fit.

## Why so many people agree so easily

There is an obvious objection. Most of the time, we do not need to meet. You and I can both look at the Moon from different continents, never talk, and still agree on where it is. Why does agreement feel automatic?

Wojciech Zurek's answer is called quantum Darwinism. The Moon is not looked at directly. It is hit by sunlight, and each photon that bounces off it carries away a tiny copy of where the Moon is. There are astronomical numbers of these copies. You catch some of them; I catch others. We never touch the Moon or each other, but we have read different copies of the same record, so we agree.

The striking part is how few copies you need. In the toy below, a system holding one bit is copied, imperfectly, into sixty small pieces of environment. Read a few percent of them and you already know the whole bit. Read more and you learn nothing new, until you hold almost all of the environment. That flat stretch is called the plateau, and it is why the world looks objective: many observers, each with a small and different fraction, all land on the same answer.

![**Figure 2.** Copies everywhere. Left: a system S scatters photons; observers A and B each catch a few different ones and never interact with S or with each other. Right: how much a fraction of the environment knows about S, for weak, medium and good copies, in an exact toy model with sixty pieces of environment. With good copies, 10% is enough to know the full bit; so is a different 10%. The second bit, a quantum correlation, needs almost the whole environment. The code is in [figs.py](figs.py).](figures/fig02.png){fig-alt="Left: a navy disc labelled S with many short arrows radiating out; two small clocks labelled A and B each receive a few amber arrows. Right: three curves of information against fraction of environment. The dark and medium ones rise steeply to 1 bit within the first 10 to 20 percent, stay flat across most of the plot, then shoot up to 2 bits at the very end. The pale curve rises slowly and has no flat stretch."}

Zurek chose the word Darwinism on purpose. Not every property of a system gets copied this well. Only some states survive being copied over and over without being disturbed, and those are the ones that become shared, objective, the same for everyone. The rest stay private, or are lost.

I find this very close to the sentence I wrote in my reply before I knew this theory: reality is not what is out there, but what survives comparison. Zurek would put it slightly differently. Reality is what survives copying. But copying is just comparison done in advance, by the environment, on everyone's behalf.

## Behind each other's horizons

The third case is the strangest, and it is the one where my "no" becomes something else.

Our universe is expanding faster and faster. One consequence is that it has a horizon, a little like a black hole turned inside out. Light that a distant galaxy emits today will never reach us, however long we wait, because the space between us grows too fast. In empty de Sitter space, the universe from the previous essay, every observer sits at the centre of their own horizon.

Now take two observers whose horizons do not overlap. Call them A and C. A can never send a message to C. C can never send one to A. They will never meet, never compare, never read copies of the same photons.

![**Figure 3.** Who can ever compare. A de Sitter universe drawn as a Penrose diagram: time goes up, light travels at 45 degrees, and the dashed red lines are horizons. A and B stay close and can exchange records: when they compare, they are consistent. A and C sit at opposite ends. Any message A sends towards C reaches the far future first. Schematic, my own; the code is in [figs.py](figs.py).](figures/fig03.png){fig-alt="A square split into four triangles by two dashed red diagonals. The left edge is a thick navy line labelled A, with a lighter curve labelled B beside it and two small arrows going back and forth between them. The right edge is an amber line labelled C. A grey dashed arrow leaves A at 45 degrees and hits the top edge before reaching C. Labels: what A can ever see, what C can ever see, far future, far past, horizons."}

Do A and C agree on one world? Here I no longer think the answer is "no." I think the question has no answer. Not an unknown answer, but no answer at all: there is no experiment, ever, by anyone, that could settle it.

Physicists have met this situation before. In 1993 Susskind, Thorlacius and Uglum proposed black hole complementarity. Someone who falls into a black hole and someone who stays outside describe what happens at the horizon in incompatible ways. The outside observer sees the infalling information smeared on the horizon and later radiated away; the falling one sees nothing special as she crosses. Both are right, the proposal says, because no one can ever hold both accounts and compare them. Susskind and Thorlacius checked a few ways one might try to cheat, for instance by having the falling observer send a message out. Every attempt failed: to arrive in time, the message would need more energy than physics allows.

So there is a kind of protection here. Contradictions are allowed, but only where nobody can catch them.

## One world, built

Put the three cases together.

- **Different sizes:** their records differ, but on what both can see, they match.
- **When they meet:** quantum mechanics makes their records consistent, and the environment often does the meeting for them.
- **Behind each other's horizons:** they can never compare, so "do they agree?" is not a question with an answer.

Nowhere in this list is there a step where the universe hands out one shared world from the start. One world is not given. It is what records build when they meet, and it extends exactly as far as meetings can reach.

This also fits the grains from the last essay. A grain that pinches off into its own closed universe counts as one state from outside, and it is everything to those inside. Now I see why those two descriptions never clash: nobody inside the grain and nobody outside it can ever compare notes. The horizon that hides the grain is also the thing that keeps both stories true.

## A short echo in the usual subject

This blog is usually about AI, so one short echo, as an analogy only. Ask two different AI models the same question and they may answer differently. There is no master copy of the right answer inside either of them. What I end up trusting is what survives comparison: two answers checked against each other, against a test, against a shared source. Agreement between machines, like agreement between observers, is not stored somewhere. It is built, each time, at the point where records meet.

## What I am not claiming

- Wigner's friend, Frauchiger–Renner and the Bong et al. experiment are about quantum mechanics without gravity. Applying them to observers in a closed universe is my own step.
- The extended Wigner's friend results are still argued over. Different interpretations escape the contradiction in different ways; I have described the relational way because it fits these essays, not because it is settled.
- The cross-perspective links rule is a postulate added to relational quantum mechanics, not something derived from it.
- Black hole complementarity is a proposal, and since the firewall argument of 2012 it has been seriously questioned. I use it as an example of the idea, not as established physics.
- The toy in Figure 2 is a textbook model with perfect symmetry. Real environments are messier, though the plateau is found in more realistic models too.
- The connection to the grains is speculation built on speculation.
